abstract: Identifying the root of eukaryotic phylogeny is integral to attempts to infer the nature of the last eukaryotic common ancestor and elucidate the prokaryote-to-eukaryote transition. However, the position of the eukaryotic root has proven difficult to resolve because of a high level of sequence divergence separating eukaryotes from their closest prokaryotic relatives, which can induce phylogenetic error in root placement. To overcome these issues, we exploit a complementary source of information: ancient gene duplications that occurred prior to the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA). For duplicated genes, each paralogue can be used to root its sibling, providing information independent of prokaryotic outgroups that can be pooled across duplicate gene families using phylogenetic reconciliation. We identified 219 pre-LECA duplicate gene families, and reconciliation analyses based on these families rejected most candidate root positions on the eukaryote tree. Most analyses favoured a root on, or within, the Metamonada, although roots on Discoba, or a deep split between Opimoda and Diphoda, were also not rejected under some conditions. The signal for an early-diverging Metamonada comes from their basal position within each paralogue in ~23-25% of duplicate gene trees, more than for other groups examined. We discuss the intriguing agreement between concatenation and reconciliation methods on the eukaryotic root, potential biases that might affect reconciliation analyses, and the implications of this credible set of roots for the nature of LECA and models of early eukaryotic evolution.
